content.text: {"relation":"REFINED","consensus_summary":"Gehenna and the lake of fire symbolize the final, post-judgment punishment of the unrepentant wicked, distinct from Sheol/Hades (the intermediate state of the dead). The dominant reading is eternal conscious torment and irreversible exclusion from God, with the imagery rooted in the Valley of Hinnom's history of child sacrifice and prophetic denunciation. Listed alternatives include annihilationism/conditional immortality, universal/restorative readings, metaphorical-separation views, and preterist/historical-judgment readings.","book_summary":"Gehenna is 'the judgment' — the valley of Hinnom outside Jerusalem where the carcases of transgressors burn (Isa 66:24), that which 'destroys both soul and body' (Matt 10:28), and explicitly distinct from Sheol, the grave that holds all alike. The framing — burning carcases, destruction of soul and body — presents Gehenna as final destruction of the wicked rather than eternal conscious torment.","consensus_core_identification":"The place/state of final divine judgment on the wicked after resurrection, distinct from Hades/Sheol, traditionally understood as eternal conscious punishment.","book_core_identification":"The final judgment that destroys the wicked entirely (soul and body), pictured as the Hinnom valley where corpses burn, distinct from Sheol the common grave.","core_relation":"BOOK_NARROWS","extension_relation":"SAME_CASES","boundary_disagreement":"The book keeps the same referent (final judgment on the wicked, distinct from Sheol/the grave) and the same set of cases (the unrepentant at final judgment), but narrows the nature of that judgment to destruction/consumption. By emphasizing 'carcases' (dead bodies, not living sufferers) and 'destroys both soul and body,' it implicitly excludes the dominant eternal-conscious-torment construal, aligning with the annihilationist/conditional-immortality alternative that all four consensus responses list as a recognized minority or common view.","material_contradiction":"","rationale":"Both readings identify Gehenna/lake of fire as the symbol of final divine judgment on the wicked, sourced in the Valley of Hinnom and distinct from Sheol/Hades — the consensus itself flags this distinction (Rev 20:14) and the book asserts it explicitly. The disagreement lies in the nature of the judgment: the consensus's primary meaning is eternal conscious torment, while the book's language (burning carcases, destroying soul and body) points to annihilation. Because the central referent and its extension are preserved and the book's position matches a well-documented listed alternative rather than replacing the consensus identification, this is a material boundary/precision disagreement, not divergence. It is more than a MATCH because the book's framing sits against the consensus's dominant construal of the punishment's nature.","citation_support":"PARTIAL","strongest_objection":"One could argue MATCH: the consensus responses themselves say the settled core is only 'final judgment on the wicked, distinct from Sheol/Hades,' with the torment-vs-destruction question explicitly unsettled; on that framing the book merely takes a listed alternative within an acknowledged open debate, not a refinement of the settled core. Alternatively, the book entry never explicitly denies eternal torment — 'fire is not quenched' language is retained — so the annihilationist reading is inferred from emphasis rather than stated.","confidence":"medium"}
